steps.body: The model renames 1/2 and 1/3 as sixths, then combines 3 sixth-size pieces and 2 sixth-size pieces to make 5/6.
steps.narration: The model renames 1/2 and 1/3 as sixths, then combines 3 sixth-size pieces and 2 sixth-size pieces to make 5/6.

widget.successFeedback: 7/12 — three twelfths and four more twelfths, counted together.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 7/12 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 7/12 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: A single twelfth is the difference between the two amounts, not their total.
12/12 is one whole; three and four twelfths fall well short of it.

predict.reveal: You are counting twelfths, so the answer is measured in twelfths too.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u add.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u add a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Once renamed, a jug holds 4/6 litre and then 1/6 litre more. Express the total as ?/6. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 names the piece size; once the pieces match, only the COUNT of them changes.
Multiplying the counts is not joining them — 4 pieces and 1 more make 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.

widget.prompt: When you add 5/12 + 5/12, what happens to the denominator?

options.label: The denominator stays 12.
options.feedback: Correct — adding counts how many same-size pieces you hold; it never re-cuts them.

options.label: The denominator becomes 24.
options.feedback: Doubling the denominator would halve every piece, changing the amount instead of counting it.

options.label: The denominator becomes 10.
options.feedback: That is the numerator of the answer — the count of pieces, not their size.

options.label: The denominator disappears.
options.feedback: Without a denominator the pieces have no size, and the answer would name nothing.
